https://www.crash.net/f1/news/1101832/1/.text: Norris described the track surface as a "lottery" Prefer Crash.Net on Google See our stories more often Add Formula 1 drivers have expressed concerns about the state of the track surface ahead of the Hungarian Grand Prix. The subject was raised during the drivers’ briefing on Friday after several complaints about track break up and poor grip conditions during practice, which led to emergency repairs overnight. But problems continued in final practice and qualifying, with drivers left unhappy and worried going into Sunday’s grand prix. Norris described the track as a "lottery" After taking pole position at the Hungaroring, Lando Norris branded the track surface as feeling “like a bit of a lottery” in some corners. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT “With the new tarmac, and it being grippy in places and not grippy in others, sometimes it feels like a bit of a lottery in certain corners,” the reigning world champion said. "The track is pretty broken up in places and there are a lot of different patches of tarmac in Turn 1 and Turn 12, I struggled to get a consistent feeling of what was best or what the car was doing every time in these kinds of corners." Williams driver Carlos Sainz was particularly critical and slammed the surface as “not to F1 standards”. “Having said that, the circuit acknowledged they were a bit caught by surprise by it when they resurfaced it,” the Spaniard added. Similar to Silverstone, similar to Jeddah, very high grip. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT “Whatever resurfacing they've done on this Turn 1, Turn 2, it is not the same quality. So they need to go back and analyse what difference there is from the 2016 tarmac to the one laid down a few months ago.” Sainz said the track surface isn't up to F1 standards Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto described the asphalt as “very bad”, while Cadillac driver Valtteri Bottas said: “They did some grinding work last night, but they didn't seem to do much. “It’s still there. It's quite easy to lock up. I had a big lock-up today. And [Turn] 13 is quite bumpy as well, so I think the track has got the feedback. The last resurface was 10 years ago.” Haas driver Ollie Bearman raised concerns about a bump at Turn 1. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT “They've resurfaced it really, really badly to be honest and we're all in agreement that they've done a really poor job,” the Briton said. “I think we're better off leaving it as it was because before it was much better. And now we have this huge bump in Turn 1, which could be interesting tomorrow, and also through Turn 13. “It's super strange. And then the track is also breaking up a lot. So the grip is poor. It's weird.” There are concerns about a repeat of June’s Monaco Grand Prix, which was red-flagged with 10 laps remaining due to the track breaking up at the final corner, where two drivers crashed. Photograph: Swedish coast guard/AFP/Getty Images Nord Stream 1 pipeline Ukrainian diver arrested in Croatia over Nord Stream pipeline bombings Berlin to seek suspect’s extradition for 2022 explosions that damaged gas pipelines to Russia Jakub Krupa Wed 19 Aug 2026 10.14 EDT Last modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 12.04 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A Ukrainian man has been arrested in Croatia as part of an investigation into the 2022 bombing of the Nord Stream gas pipelines between Germany and Russia. Undersea explosions in September 2022, just months after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine , damaged three of the four pipelines built to carry Russian fossil gas to Germany under the Baltic Sea. The man, a trained scuba diver who prosecutors allege was directly involved in the explosions, was arrested in the Croatian seaside town of Pula on Wednesday. Berlin will seek his extradition to face trial at the federal court in Karlsruhe, in Germany . The German prosecutor’s office said the suspect “belonged to a group of people, including the separately prosecuted Serhiy K, who planted explosives near the island of Bornholm in September 2022 on the Nord Stream 1 and Nord Stream 2 gas pipelines. View image in fullscreen The landfall facilities of the Nord Stream 1 gas pipeline in Lubmin, Germany. Photograph: Hannibal Hanschke/Reuters “The accused participated in the necessary dives,” it added. Prosecutors identified the suspect only as Vladimir Z, but he is understood to be the same man arrested by Poland last year – and released after a Polish court ruled against executing a European arrest warrant issued by Germany. He was identified in that court as Volodymyr Zhuravlev. In a landmark ruling that caused friction in Polish-German relations, the Polish court argued that Germany had no jurisdiction in the case, and that the destruction of Nord Stream could be seen as a justified action by Ukraine as part of a defensive war. View image in fullscreen The man arrested in Croatia is understood to be Volodymyr Zhuravlev (centre), who appeared in a Polish court and was later released. Photograph: Rafał Guz/EPA The ruling aligned with Poland’s longstanding opposition to the pipeline project, seen as a symbol of Berlin’s close relations with Russia , with the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, publicly saying that “the problem with Nord Stream 2 is not that it was blown up; the problem is that it was built”. The Nord Stream riddle: echoes of mistrust ripple through Europe Read more Polish and German media reported that the suspect had evaded arrest in Poland in 2024, fleeing back to Ukraine. Polish authorities blamed Germany for administrative errors when logging him into the international wanted database, which allowed him to cross the border despite an active arrest warrant. The German magazine Der Spiegel alleged the suspect was helped to escape by a Ukrainian military attache stationed in Warsaw. The man’s second arrest – this time in Croatia – highlights Berlin’s determination to bring him in front of German courts, despite awkwardness given Russia’s aggression against Ukraine and Germany’s longstanding help for Kyiv. The other suspect, Serhiy K, was arrested in Italy last August and extradited to Germany in November, after unsuccessful appeals in Italian courts. Share it with your friends! Facebook Twitter Google Pinterest Reddit Email LinkedIn Romania’s centrist parliamentary parties failed to reach an agreement on the draft unitary wage law for public sector employees during talks convened by president Nicușor Dan on August 11, according to sources cited by G4Media . The deadlock puts at risk EUR 771 million in grants under the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF), as the legislation is a milestone that must be adopted by August 31. The talks brought together president Dan and the leaders of the Social Democratic Party (PSD), National Liberal Party (PNL), Save Romania Union (USR) and Democratic Alliance of Hungarians in Romania (UDMR), amid disagreements over the reform of public sector pay. Formally, a major obstacle is the financial impact of demands made by trade unions, which are supported by the PSD, according to the cited sources. Separately, analysts argue that a more transparent and consistent framework for remuneration across the public sector could reduce the influence of trade unions, political leaders and senior public officials over discretionary bonuses and other supplements that have contributed to the complexity of the current pay structure. The parties are continuing negotiations in an effort to find a formula that would allow the milestone to be completed by the deadline. One option under discussion is to submit the draft law to Parliament next week or, at the latest, within two weeks, leaving limited time for its adoption before August 31. The negotiations follow repeated warnings from the government that the deadline for completing the RRF milestone is approaching. Interim Labour Minister Dragoș Pîslaru said on August 10 that this was the final week in which a political agreement could be reached in time for the reform to be adopted and promulgated by the end of August. https://praguemonitor.com/work-life/aver.text: Czechia Business Prague Housing Europe & World Work & Life Briefings Key points CZK 48,967 is the average wage the government uses for 2026 tax and insurance thresholds; the Czech Statistical Office publishes the average and median wage by region and sector, and Prague sits above the national figure. On a hypothetical employee earning exactly CZK 48,967 gross a month, with the standard credit and no children, take-home pay is about CZK 38,500. The employer's own contributions (24.8% social and 9% health) sit on top of gross pay and never reach the employee's payslip. On this page 7 sections Three numbers called "the average" Mean or median From gross to net What the net figure has to cover Pay that is not a salary Who earns more, and why A practical next step Search for the average salary in Prague and you will find a number. Look for where it came from and you may find three: a statutory figure used to set tax thresholds, a statistical average of gross wages in one region, and a job-portal estimate of what advertised posts pay. They are not the same, they are not for the same people, and only one of them is what lands in a bank account. This article separates them, runs the gross-to-net arithmetic on a hypothetical employee and shows how to compare take-home pay with local costs. It quotes no market rent or price, because those are tied to a date and a district. For the budget side, see can you live on a Czech average salary in Prague and the monthly cost of living breakdown . Three numbers called "the average" The statutory average wage. The government sets an average wage for each year, and a number of thresholds follow from it. For 2026 it is CZK 48,967 (as of 2026; check the Financial Administration). The higher income tax rate begins at 36 times this figure, and several insurance thresholds are defined as a share of it. It is a policy parameter, calculated in a particular way, and not a survey of what Prague employers pay. The statistical average. The Czech Statistical Office publishes average gross monthly wages by region, by sector and by quarter, along with medians. Prague's regional figure is above the national one, because the capital has a higher concentration of finance, IT, headquarters and public administration jobs. The size of the gap changes each quarter, so we give no number; open the current table. The advertised wage. Job portals and recruiters publish salary ranges for particular posts. These are useful for a specific job and misleading as an average, since they reflect who advertises, not who works. The Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs also runs an earnings information system with figures by occupation, which is a better guide to a given profession. Mean or median The average, or mean, is pulled upward by high earners. The median is the wage in the middle: half of employees earn less, half more. In a wage distribution with a long upper tail the median is below the mean, so "the average person" earns less than the average. For a newcomer comparing offers, the median by occupation is more informative than the all-sector mean. The Czech Statistical Office publishes both, and the explanation of how it measures them is in what the statistics office publishes . From gross to net The employee pays social insurance of 7.1% (6.5% for pensions and 0.6% for sickness) and health insurance of 4.5%. Income tax is 15% of gross pay (rounded up to the next hundred crowns for the monthly advance), less the taxpayer credit of CZK 2,570 a month. The employer pays 24.8% for social insurance and 9% for health insurance on top, which never appears as a deduction (as of 2026; check ČSSZ and the Financial Administration). Two hypothetical employees, both on the standard credit with no children: Gross to net for two hypothetical employees, 2026 (CZK a month) Line At the average wage At the minimum wage Gross pay 48,967 22,400 Social insurance, employee (7.1%) −3,477 −1,591 Health insurance, employee (4.5%) −2,204 −1,008 Income tax, 15% less credit of 2,570 −4,780 −790 Take-home pay about 38,506 about 19,011 Hypothetical calculation using 2026 rates; contributions rounded up to whole crowns and the tax base rounded up to the next hundred crowns, as payroll does. Children, other credits and deductions are not included. Check the Financial Administration and ČSSZ. The first column is the statutory average wage. Taking 13.5% in contributions and 15% in tax, less the credit, leaves about 78.6% of gross. The second is the statutory minimum wage of CZK 22,400 (2026), where the credit absorbs most of the tax, so the employee keeps about 85% of gross. The employer's side makes the cost of the first employee larger than the payslip suggests. At the average wage, social insurance of 24.8% adds about CZK 12,100 and health insurance of 9% adds about CZK 4,400, so the employer's total cost is roughly CZK 65,500 for a gross wage of CZK 48,967. The arithmetic: 48,967 × 24.8% = 12,144; 48,967 × 9% = 4,407; the sum with gross is 65,518. See employer contributions if you are on the other side of the table. What the net figure has to cover Take-home pay is where the household budget begins. The question that follows is how much of it a particular cost takes. Each ten percentage points of the net pay in the first column is about CZK 3,850. A household spending 40% of take-home pay on housing and its running costs is spending about CZK 15,400 on it, and the remaining 60% has to cover food, transport, insurance, phone, savings and the rest. That is the method. The inputs are yours: the real full monthly cost of a flat you would take, including service charges and energy. We do not supply a Prague rent, because an average rent is a poor guide to the flat you would actually rent. Look at current listings in the districts you are considering, and use our guide to renting a flat as a foreigner to check what a quoted rent includes. Test a salary against Prague costs Start from the gross offer Check whether it is monthly or annual, and whether bonuses or a thirteenth salary are guaranteed in the contract. Convert to net Apply 7.1% social, 4.5% health and 15% tax less CZK 2,570 as above, adjusting for children and other credits. Price housing in full Rent plus service charges plus energy plus internet, for a flat you would actually take. Add fixed costs Transport pass, insurance, phone and any loan payments. See what is left Divide the remainder by the weeks in the month. That is the number you live on. Pay that is not a salary The calculation above is for an employee on a standard contract. Other arrangements change the net figure. Work under an agreement to complete a job (DPP) is capped at 300 hours a year per employer, and insurance is due only when earnings from one employer reach CZK 12,000 a month in 2026. Below that, and without a signed tax declaration, the employer withholds 15%. Work under an agreement to perform work (DPČ) triggers insurance from CZK 4,500 a month (as of 2026; check ČSSZ and the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs). Freelancers pay their own contributions and tax, with minimum advances that apply whatever the income. Our explainers on DPP and DPČ and on social security contributions set out the differences. Who earns more, and why Wage levels in Prague differ by sector far more than by city. A headline average blends senior software engineers, public sector nurses and shop assistants. A job in a headquarters function in the capital often pays more than the same job elsewhere in Czechia; a job in the public sector follows national pay scales. The practical advice is to compare like with like: the same occupation and seniority, in the same region, from the same source. For a buyer, the wage is also the input to a mortgage assessment. A bank looks at net income, existing obligations and household costs, and the borrowing estimator on Hypoteky.com gives a rough picture of what that implies for the size of a loan. For the longer horizon, the buy or rent calculator compares paths. Ask for the gross annual package When comparing offers, ask whether the figure is a monthly gross wage, whether a thirteenth salary or bonus is guaranteed, and whether benefits such as a pension contribution or a meal allowance are included. Two offers with the same monthly figure can differ by thousands over a year. Frequently asked questions What is the average salary in Prague? The Czech Statistical Office publishes the current regional average gross wage, which is above the national figure. The number moves each quarter, so use the latest release. The CZK 48,967 often quoted is the statutory average for 2026 thresholds, not a Prague survey. How much is CZK 48,967 gross after tax? About CZK 38,500 for a hypothetical employee with the standard taxpayer credit and no children, after 7.1% social, 4.5% health insurance and 15% tax less CZK 2,570 (as of 2026). Does the employer pay anything extra? Yes. The employer pays 24.8% social and 9% health insurance on top of the gross wage, which never appears on the employee's payslip. Is the minimum wage enough to live on in Prague? The statutory minimum is CZK 22,400 a month in 2026. Whether it covers a household depends on housing costs and household size, which is the subject of our budget scenarios article. A practical next step Take a real salary offer, run it through the net-pay steps above, and subtract the full cost of one real flat. The result will tell you more about your situation than any average. This is a general explainer, not legal, tax or mortgage advice. https://www.ynetnews.com/article/r1e1hib.text: Israel's diplomatic standing in Europe is at a historic low, and as if that were not enough, Saturday afternoon brought an attack on European diplomats by Jewish rioters. Once again, security forces failed to arrive at the scene in time, and the suspects fled without being arrested. "They were attacked by seven adult men, ages 20 and older, who apparently did not come from a nearby outpost but from farther away, meaning they had been specifically summoned," one of the diplomats present at the scene said. "They kicked the French mayor, and he was injured." A European diplomat who was in one of the vehicles targeted in the attack described the terrifying moments to ynet. "The residents of Taybeh invited diplomats and peace activists to the olive harvest to protect them. At one point, we heard that settlers were approaching, so we immediately got into the car and started driving. Then I saw masked settlers carrying sticks and metal crowbars running toward us. It was clear they had no good intentions. It was frightening. They hadn't come to pick olives." "They kicked the French mayor, and after beating him, they shouted 'Viva la France.' They had recognized the French flag," the diplomat continued. "They also attacked the Belgian vehicle. When you see something like that, you say to yourself, 'My God, how can something like this happen?' We came with security personnel, and it's absurd because this is an area under Israeli control. We knew settler violence was serious, but when you witness it firsthand, you understand just how terrible it is, especially for the residents who depend on the olive harvest for their livelihoods." The mayor is Bernard Baudoux of Aulnoye-Aymeries, France, a member of the French Communist Party. The attack itself, which took place in the Christian village of Taybeh in the Binyamin region of the West Bank, was not captured on camera. However, Baudoux was subsequently filmed lying on the ground, and a vehicle belonging to the Belgian Consulate was photographed with a smashed window. "This was professional-style violence, far more severe than anything we have seen in previous incidents," the diplomat said, emphasizing that all members of the delegation were "convinced" it was "an organized operation intended to send a message to Europeans, rather than to local residents." The diplomat said members of the delegation were deeply angered by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's response to the incident. Netanyahu has so far refrained from explicitly addressing the attack, as have the leaders of other parties in his political camp. However, the Prime Minister's Office issued a statement in English casting doubt on the European account, even after Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar and the IDF said "Israeli rioters" were responsible for the incident. Beyond the fact that Israel is once again presenting conflicting messages to the international community, with its own officials contradicting one another, the diplomat said, "The mayor's political background is irrelevant to the question of who attacked him. Netanyahu's statement completely ignores the fact that this is a Christian village and that the delegation came from Catholic countries that consider themselves committed to protecting Christians in the West Bank. In Europe, Netanyahu's statement is seen as shocking." 'This was an attack with clubs' Members of the European delegation also responded to claims made in Israel that the visit should have been coordinated with security forces so they could provide protection for participants. Unlike the leaders of parties in Netanyahu's political camp, Ofer Winter's Amcha Yisrael party condemned the attack. In ynet's "No Man's Land" series, Rabbi Benny Lau noted that the Christian population between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea has been steadily declining and now accounts for less than 1% of the Palestinian population in the area. Signs of this exodus are visible in the village's empty homes. Since October 7, 15 families have left Taybeh and the country, relocating to places where substantial communities of Taybeh expatriates have already established themselves. Father Jacques, one of the local church leaders, described to Lau how despair has been taking hold among residents. He spoke nostalgically about the years before the Second Intifada and the Oslo Accords, when, he recalled, he could get into his car and drive to Jaffa, while settlers would stop in the village to buy popsicles and ice cream for their children. The settlement of Ofra lies west of Taybeh, and numerous settler farms have been established around the village in recent years. Christian tradition identifies Taybeh with the ancient town of Ephraim, where Jesus stayed with his disciples before traveling to Jerusalem. The village is therefore considered a holy site and is home to historic churches and Christian institutions. Taybeh is also home to the brewery that has produced Taybeh Beer, the first Palestinian beer, since 1995. The village hosts an Oktoberfest-style beer festival that typically attracts Europeans visiting the region. Since 2025, Taybeh has been subjected to several attacks by Jewish rioters, including incidents in which vehicles and homes were set on fire. Several Palestinians have also been killed by live gunfire. In one incident in July 2025, rioters set fire to a cemetery and desecrated a church, prompting Huckabee to visit the village and describe the incident as an act of terrorism. But even after that visit, settlers continued their attacks, setting Palestinian vehicles on fire and spray-painting graffiti that read, "You will regret this."
